notes.meaning: Manasseh was Joseph's oldest son, so his tribe received a full share of the land. The family of Machir, Manasseh's firstborn son, had already received Gilead and Bashan on the east side of the Jordan River. Machir's descendants were skilled and brave warriors, making them well suited to guard that dangerous border country.

Land west of the Jordan River was assigned to the rest of the clans of Manasseh. These six family lines came down through Gilead, Machir's son. Each of these male family lines was given its own portion in the promised land.

Zelophehad belonged to the clan of Hepher, but he died leaving five daughters and no sons. In ancient Israel, family property normally passed only to sons so that land would stay within the clan. These five women—Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah—faced the danger of losing their family's name and portion.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars argue that this story was a later legal invention written to justify changing earlier inheritance laws so daughters could inherit property when there were no sons.

notes.meaning: The daughters came before Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the tribal leaders to ask for their share. They reminded Joshua that the Lord had directly commanded Moses to give them land among their relatives. Joshua honored God's command and gave them an inheritance, showing that God's promises belonged to them just as much as to their male cousins.

Because of this ruling, western Manasseh was divided into ten distinct shares. Five portions went to the five surviving male clans, and five portions went to the five daughters of Zelophehad to represent their father. This gave the tribe ten portions in Canaan in addition to the territory already settled east of the Jordan.

Zelophehad's daughters received their estates right alongside the male heads of families. The text notes that the rest of the tribe, descending from Machir, had already settled in the fertile region of Gilead. God made sure that no family line within the tribe was left without land.

Manasseh's southern border started from the town of Asher and ran toward Michmethath, near the city of Shechem. From there, the border moved south toward the spring and settlement of En-tappuah. This line marked the boundary between Manasseh and its brother tribe Ephraim.

The countryside surrounding Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the walled town of Tappuah itself was given to Ephraim. Dividing land this way meant the two brother tribes had to live close together and cooperate daily. It reminded both tribes that they shared a common family bond under God.

The border ran down to the Brook of Kanah and continued west all the way to the Mediterranean Sea. Ephraim was given several towns located inside Manasseh's territory north of the brook. Even with separate borders, the two tribes of Joseph were closely woven together across the region.

Ephraim's territory lay to the south of the brook, while Manasseh's land stretched to the north. Manasseh reached the Mediterranean Sea on the west and met the borders of Asher on the north and Issachar on the east. Together, the two tribes of Joseph formed a large, connected territory in central Canaan.

Manasseh was also given several major towns and settlements that lay within the borders of Issachar and Asher. These included important fortress towns like Beth-shean, Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo, along with the coastal town of Dor. These fortified positions guarded important valleys and trade routes across northern Canaan.

The people of Manasseh failed to drive out the Canaanite residents from these strong valley cities. The Canaanites dug in their heels and were determined to stay in the land. Manasseh lacked the faith and courage needed to finish taking the ground God had promised them.

Later, when Israel grew stronger, they still did not drive out the Canaanites as God had ordered. Instead, they forced them to do hard labor and pay taxes for their own financial benefit. This compromise seemed practical at the time, but it directly broke God's law and later led Israel into idol worship.

The tribes of Joseph came together and complained to Joshua that they had received only one lot despite their large numbers. They pointed out how greatly the Lord had blessed them with population growth. They felt their allotment was too small and expected special favors from Joshua, who belonged to their tribe.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest this complaint shows that the oldest traditions knew nothing of Manasseh holding land east of the Jordan, proposing that the eastern settlement happened later.

notes.meaning: Joshua refused to show favoritism to his own people and gave them a practical answer. He told them that if they were truly so numerous, they should go up into the thick mountain forests of the Perizzites and Rephaim. By clearing the trees, they could create plenty of new farmland and living space for themselves.

The people of Joseph made excuses to avoid the hard work Joshua suggested. They argued that the hill country was not enough for them, and they feared the Canaanites in the valley who had iron war chariots. Their fear of enemy weapons blinded them to what God had promised to do for them.

Joshua stood firm and repeated that they were indeed a great and powerful people. He agreed that their large numbers meant they should have more than just one cleared share of land. However, the extra territory would come through their own hard work and courage in battle rather than an easy gift.

Joshua assured them that the entire forested mountain would belong to them once they cleared the trees. He promised that even though the Canaanites were strong and drove iron chariots, God would give them the power to drive the enemy out. Trusting God means moving forward in faith to face obstacles that look impossible to conquer alone.
